source: Peters, Zhang, Jiao, Li, Zhou, Lissitz (2025) Text-Based Approaches to Item Difficulty Modeling in Large-Scale Assessments: A Systematic Review
finding: Review of 37 studies to May 2025. Text-based difficulty prediction works moderately, and the spread across studies is huge.
numbers: Pearson r over 17 values: 0.04 to 0.87, mean 0.545 (SD 0.225). R2 over 13 values: 0.208 to 0.788, mean 0.478. RMSE on p-value 0.165-0.268 (mean 0.216, 6 studies); on Rasch b 0.354-1.295 (mean 0.740, 8 studies). Exact classification accuracy 0.325-0.806 (mean 0.567, 3 studies).
limits: Metrics, scales and datasets differ between studies, so numbers are not directly comparable. Best values come from small or in-sample sets.
agent_relevance: Plan on a modest cheap difficulty signal (r about 0.5) for S0, not a precise one. Treat the best published numbers as ceilings.

source: Peters et al. (2025) review, citing Conejo et al. (2014) and Loukina et al. (2016)
finding: Human expert ratings and classic linguistic features are weak predictors of difficulty.
numbers: Conejo et al. (2014): expert ratings versus IRT difficulty correlation as low as 0.38. Loukina et al. (2016): over 100 linguistic features with random forest gave r = 0.50 with CTT delta.
limits: The primary papers (Conejo, Loukina) were not opened; numbers are taken from the review text.
agent_relevance: A cheap proxy for S0 has to beat r about 0.4-0.5 to be worth more than a human guess.

source: Razavi & Powers (2025) Estimating Item Difficulty Using Large Language Models and Tree-Based Machine Learning Algorithms
finding: On 5,170 K-5 maths and reading items, asking an LLM for one difficulty number works fairly well. Having the LLM extract features and feeding them to a random forest works better.
numbers: Maths direct estimate: r = .83, RMSE 0.91 (dummy 1.01). Reading direct: r about .81, RMSE 0.86. Feature-based random forest, maths: r = .87, RMSE 0.83 (TF-IDF+RF 1.01; metadata-only RF 1.12). Direct estimate was worse than the grade-mean dummy in grade K.
limits: One vendor item bank. Regression fitted on a training split. Pooled across grades, so grade level carries much of r.
agent_relevance: Structured feature extraction by the model, then a code-side regressor, beats asking the model for a number. This fits the rule that code decides.

source: Razavi & Powers (2025), grade-level breakdown
finding: Part of the headline correlation is between-grade variance. Within a grade the prediction is weaker and sometimes no better than the grade mean.
numbers: Within-grade feature-model r from .37 to .70. Grade 1 direct estimate improved RMSE and MAE over dummy by only 0.01. Grade K feature model was worse than dummy in maths.
limits: Pooled r overstates discrimination within one task family.
agent_relevance: Judge an S0 estimator within task families of similar type, not on a pooled range that mixes easy and hard families.

source: Zotos, de Jong, Valdenegro-Toro, Sburlea, Nissim, van Rijn (2025) NLP Methods May Actually Be Better Than Professors at Estimating Question Difficulty
finding: Professors were poor at predicting how many students would answer true/false questions correctly. Gemini 2.5 direct estimates did better. A small SVM trained on LLM uncertainty did best.
numbers: Four professors, two exams (Neural Networks, about 47 training items; Advanced ML, about 42). Three of four professors had no useful rank correlation on Neural Networks (best rho = 0.211). Averaging professor estimates did not help. SVM with TF-IDF plus LLM uncertainties: Spearman 0.853 (NN). SVM with uncertainties only: 0.582 (AML).
limits: Tiny test splits (about 10 items). One lab, true/false only. Professors saw one labelled example while the regressor trained on dozens, as the authors note.
agent_relevance: Supports using the model's own uncertainty as an S0 feature. A training set of about 40 items is within reach of per-domain calibration.

source: Zotos, van Rijn, Nissim (2025) Are You Doubtful? Oh, It Might Be Difficult Then! Model uncertainty for question difficulty estimation
finding: Adding LLM uncertainty features to text features in a random forest cut error on all three MCQ sets and gave state of the art on USMLE and CMCQRD.
numbers: RMSE dummy vs best: Biopsychology 0.1667 vs about 0.136; USMLE 0.3110 vs 0.2817-0.2862 (best literature 0.291); CMCQRD 0.1833 vs about 0.165. Linguistic-features baseline: 0.1544 and 0.3147. Standard deviation over ten runs at most 0.002. BEA 2024 shared task: best team beat baseline RMSE by only 0.012; top 10 within 0.009.
limits: Gains are small in absolute terms (about 0.02-0.03 RMSE). Student selection rate is the label in most sets.
agent_relevance: Uncertainty is a real but small signal. Do not expect large gains from any S0 difficulty estimate on knowledge items.

source: Zotos, van Rijn, Nissim (2025) Can Model Uncertainty Function as a Proxy for MCQ Item Difficulty?
finding: Correlation between LLM uncertainty (first-token probability, choice-order sensitivity) and student answer distributions is present but weak. It depends on question type and on whether the model answered correctly.
numbers: 451 Biopsychology questions. Choice-entropy correlations weak to moderate. Chi-squared tests (441 questions) show every model distribution differs significantly from the student distribution.
limits: Small open models (for example Llama3-8B, Mistral-7B). Question types have few items each.
agent_relevance: Uncertainty behaves differently for right and wrong answers, so split any difficulty signal by whether the answer passed a check.

source: Li, Chen, Xiao, Chen, Jiao, Zhou (2026) Can LLMs Estimate Student Struggles? Human-AI Difficulty Alignment with Proficiency Simulation
finding: Over 20 models on four datasets: models do not agree with human difficulty rankings, bigger or reasoning models are not better, and models agree with each other more than with humans (machine consensus).
numbers: Zero-shot Spearman averages below 0.50. SAT Math about 0.41, USMLE about 0.13. GPT-5 rho 0.34 vs GPT-4.1 0.44. Predictions bunch at low difficulty (variance collapse). Ensembling helps then hurts: SAT Math 0.56 rising to a peak of 0.66, then dilution once the pool passes K = 14 models.
limits: Four datasets (USMLE, Cambridge, SAT Reading, SAT Math). Zero-shot prompts.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a model's stated difficulty. Strong models underrate difficulty because items are easy for them. Use code-side signals.

source: Li et al. (2026), curse of knowledge and metacognitive blind spot
finding: Difficulty derived from the models' own correctness (IRT over 21 models) matches human difficulty even worse than their stated estimates. Models cannot be role-played down to a weaker student.
numbers: USMLE: Savant Rate 70.4% (hard-for-human items solved by over 90% of models), saturation 75.6%. SAT Math: Savant Rate 32.2%, saturation 54.6%, rho 0.386. Proficiency persona changed accuracy by under 1%. AUROC of model confidence for its own errors mostly 0.50-0.60, with highs of 0.73 (GPT-5, Cambridge) and 0.64 (DeepSeek-R1, USMLE).
limits: Human difficulty is for human test takers. The divergence is partly a ceiling effect on items that are easy for models.
agent_relevance: The model's difficulty differs from a human's. For our agent the target is difficulty for the model itself, so measure by sampling or hidden states, not by human-style features.

source: Acquaye, Huang, Carpuat, Rudinger (2026) Take Out Your Calculators: Estimating the Real Difficulty of Question Items with LLM Student Simulations
finding: Direct difficulty prompting fails on 631 NAEP maths items. Simulating a class of role-played students and fitting IRT works much better.
numbers: Direct prompting correlations -0.139 to 0.137 (GPT-4o rho 0.01-0.15). Simulation correlations up to 0.75, 0.76, 0.82 for grades 4, 8, 12; range across models 0.40-0.78. Gemma-2-27b grade 12 r = 0.78. Class of 300 (75/105/75/45 by proficiency). Llama-3.3-70b (92% accurate) simulated poorly; Qwen2.5-32B r = 0.51-0.62; Gemma-2-9b equalled 27b at grade 4 (r 0.69 each). Diverse names raised r (0.60-0.72 vs 0.57-0.67).
limits: Maths multiple choice only, NAEP released items, success rate as label. Li et al. found persona simulation unstable, the difference being that this paper aggregates many simulated responses.
agent_relevance: A cheap difficulty signal for S0 comes from many sampled attempts, not one judgement. Weaker models can simulate difficulty better.

source: Acquaye et al. (2026), class size trade-off
finding: Going from 100 to 300 simulated students adds little. Small classes suffice for quick iteration.
numbers: Authors suggest n = 50 for rapid iteration. The gain from 100 to 300 is marginal.
limits: Reported within one dataset family.
agent_relevance: A few tens of cheap probe samples can already give a usable difficulty rank.

source: Scarlatos, Fernandez, Ormerod, Lottridge, Lan (2025) SMART: Simulated Students Aligned with IRT for Question Difficulty Prediction
finding: Training a simulator with DPO on IRT-based preference pairs beats zero-shot simulation and some direct predictors on open-ended items.
numbers: Smarter Balanced (Llama-3.2-1B): SMART PCC 0.649, SCC 0.486, RMSE 0.670; zero-shot simulation PCC 0.265. kNN mean over SBERT: PCC 0.596, SCC 0.522, RMSE 0.681. CodeWorkout: SMART PCC 0.308 (1B), 0.393 (3B); zero-shot simulation 0.073. In-context random 70B on Smarter Balanced: PCC 0.12.
limits: On Smarter Balanced a simple kNN baseline had a higher rank correlation than SMART at 1B. Needs training, so not a scaffold-only method.
agent_relevance: Simple nearest-neighbour baselines are strong. A scaffold can reuse the recorded difficulty of similar past items.

source: Wang, Li, Zeng, Li, Jiao, Zhou, Zhou (2026) Cognitive Episodes in LLM Reasoning Traces Enable Interpretable Human Item Difficulty Prediction (Epi2Diff)
finding: Features from a reasoning model's trace (effort, how it is spread over problem-solving states, transitions) predict human difficulty better than item text alone.
numbers: 8.1% average relative gain over supervised LLM fine-tuning on SAT-derived classification. Baselines: SLM fine-tune SAT Math accuracy about 0.60-0.64; USMLE R2 0.03-0.08, RMSE about 0.30. Prompted LLMs gave negative R2: GPT-5 zero-shot on Cambridge R2 -10.8 (RMSE 33.7), GPT-4o zero-shot on USMLE R2 -0.25. Harder items show more iterative, implementation-heavy episodes, not just longer text. Episode labeler accuracy 0.799.
limits: Costs a full solve attempt. Datasets of 800-1,300 items. Gains over the best baselines are modest.
agent_relevance: Process cost of a first solve attempt (length, iterations) is a usable difficulty signal, so S0 can follow a cheap first attempt.

source: Wang, Jiao, Li, Peters, Choi, Zhou, Xu (2026) Can LLMs Really Understand Item Difficulty Levels?
finding: On a large-scale Reading and Writing test, LLM prompting for 3-level difficulty trails a fine-tuned encoder. Stronger models underestimate difficulty more.
numbers: Best LLM: zero-shot GPT-4.1, temperature 0, QWK 0.578, accuracy 0.618 (prompt-strategy comparison). In the model comparison GPT-4.1 had QWK 0.447, accuracy 0.535, beating GPT-5.4. ConvBERT QWK 0.625. Best feature-based model QWK 0.549 with 40% linguistic features. GPT-5 best at minimal reasoning effort (QWK 0.41). Few-shot helped GPT-5 but not GPT-4.1. Embeddings of the three levels overlap.
limits: One test, three classes. LLM QWK varies by setting.
agent_relevance: Item text alone does not separate difficulty. A check must come from behaviour on the item.

source: Brant, Kuhn, Pang (2026) Estimating Exam Item Difficulty with LLMs: A Benchmark on Brazil's ENEM Corpus
finding: Ten LLMs against official IRT parameters on 1,031 items: rank agreement is weak to moderate, difficulty is underestimated, and visual items do worse.
numbers: Best prompt per model Spearman about 0.10-0.37 (o3 0.37, Gemini-2.5-Flash 0.35, Claude-4-Sonnet 0.33). A mean predictor had RMSE 1.19 and rho 0. Visual items: RMSE higher by 1.26 (SD 0.95) than non-visual in 56 of 76 model-prompt pairs (p < 0.05), Hedges g = -0.17. Reasoning prompts raised rho by up to 0.19 for open-weight models but not for GPT-4o.
limits: Visuals were converted to text, so the penalty may be transcription loss. Low RMSE can come from regressing to the mean.
agent_relevance: Report rank correlation and error together. A predictor that outputs the mean looks good on error and is useless for ranking.

source: Kolesnikova, Fedyanin, Hofman, Brinkhuis, Bolsinova (2026) Estimating Item Difficulty with Large Language Models as Experts
finding: In a full factorial test on primary maths items, pairwise comparison beats absolute rating. Token probabilities plus labelled examples lift absolute rating to a similar level.
numbers: Three LLMs, six maths domains, Spearman moderate to strong. Pairwise beats absolute in most configurations, with the largest gain in zero-shot hard decisions. Exceptions where the 95% bootstrap interval includes zero: few-shot soft for GPT-4o and DeepSeek Chat. Cited priors: Zotos direct rho .052-.345; Raina soft probabilities lifted rho from .41 to .48.
limits: Primary maths from one learning platform. Exact table values were not recorded by this reader.
agent_relevance: To rank which of two items is harder, use a pairwise comparison counted in code, not an absolute number.

source: Zhu, Liu, Lin, Tong, Zhong, Shao (2025) The LLM Already Knows: Estimating LLM-Perceived Question Difficulty via Hidden Representations
finding: The target model's own initial hidden state, before it writes anything, predicts whether it will fail. Using this to set the sampling budget saves tokens.
numbers: ScienceQA ROC-AUC 93.09%, Macro-F1 79.48%. Cross-domain transfer shows a notable drop in ROC-AUC and Macro-F1. Applied to Self-Consistency, Best-of-N and Self-Refine, it gave similar or better accuracy with fewer generated tokens.
limits: Needs white-box access and a trained value function per model. Not usable through an API.
agent_relevance: A zero-token S0 for an open-weight model. For a prompt-only agent the substitute is a cheap probe sample.

source: Jain, Hollander, He, Tang, Zhang, Sabatini (2025) Exploring the Potential of LLMs for Estimating Reading Comprehension Question Difficulty
finding: GPT-4o and o1 answered nearly all SARA reading questions correctly while human accuracy was 81.7%-89.8% by subtest. Their difficulty estimates follow IRT difficulty but are compressed.
numbers: Human accuracy 81.7% (Word Recognition and Decoding) to 89.8% (Reading Efficiency). o1 estimates were more compressed than GPT-4o. Both under-represented extreme IRT values.
limits: No correlation figure was recorded by this reader. One reading battery.
agent_relevance: Extreme-difficulty items are where estimates fail first.

source: Sun, Liu, Luo (2019) Automatic Generation of Number Series Reasoning Items of High Difficulty (LLTM)
finding: A feature-based LLTM predicted Rasch difficulty of generated number-series items very well, in-sample.
numbers: 92 generated items (7 dropped), 466 students. LLTM with 10 features explained 77% of variance (r = .88). At the 18 item-model level r = .97. Two-step items mean difficulty 1.28 vs -0.70 for one-step. Ability correlated 0.70 (disattenuated) with a 5-item Raven subset (alpha .612).
limits: In-sample fit on the same data. Small sample from one city. About 23% of variance left unexplained within item models.
agent_relevance: Rule-structured items (like ARC-type tasks) are where feature-based difficulty works best. Free-text knowledge items are not.

source: Yang, Sanyal, Michelson, Ainooson, Kunda (2022) Automatic Item Generation of Figural Analogy Problems (on Embretson 1998 and Carpenter 1990)
finding: History of matrix difficulty modelling: rule count and type explained part of difficulty, and Embretson added perceptual features.
numbers: Early human experiments: three cognitive-operation dimensions explained roughly 40% of item difficulty; 60% unexplained, with numbers of elements and rules a further source. Embretson added three binary perceptual features (object overlay, fusion, distortion). Her ITEMGEN software is no longer easily accessible.
limits: Secondary description. The Embretson (1998) and Carpenter (1990) primary papers were not opened. The 40% figure is an early study cited in the review.
agent_relevance: For puzzle items, rule count and perceptual complexity are the first feature set. Our own item metadata can mimic this.

source: Yang et al. (2022), generator coverage
finding: Most generators copy Carpenter's five rules and the 3x3 format. Perceptual organization is a missing factor in made-up items.
numbers: MatrixDeveloper (Hofer 2004) covers 4x4 matrices and was used in several psychometric studies (Freund 2008; Freund and Holling 2011). The PGM and RAVEN datasets inherit the Carpenter rules.
limits: Review text only.
agent_relevance: ARC-like benchmarks for models share this structure, so rule-count features transfer in form.

source: Peters et al. (2025) review, feature engineering versus learned representations
finding: Hand-built features give interpretable but domain-bound models. Language-model features need less engineering. With small data, engineered features beat BERT embeddings in one case.
numbers: One study: engineered linguistic features RMSE 0.302 vs fine-tuned BERT embeddings 0.614. Another: 5-7% RMSE reduction over BERT baselines on large-scale maths items.
limits: Mixed results across studies. No pooled effect size.
agent_relevance: With few labelled items, a small hand-picked feature set can beat a large learned representation.

source: Peters et al. (2025) review, evaluation practice
finding: Studies use many different metrics, which blocks comparison.
numbers: RMSE in 31.8% of metric uses, Pearson 19.3%, R2 about 14.8%, Spearman 4.5%; 18 unique metrics. USMLE shared-task studies use transformed p-value (RMSE 0.253-0.308).
limits: Counts as stated in the review's tables.
agent_relevance: Pick one rank metric and one error metric for our S0 tests and report both.

source: Random-effects LLTM and adaptive testing simulation (Frontiers in Psychology 2024)
finding: A simulation shows that predicting difficulty from design features alone is worse than calibration unless the features explain a large part of difficulty variance.
numbers: 1,000 simulated examinees, 300 items in 30 families, adaptive test length 60, 50 replications per condition. R2 set at 60/70/80/90% (residual variance 1.494/0.961/0.560/0.249). LLTM RMSE above the calibrated Rasch model at test length 30 at every R2. Matching precision at RMSE 0.4 needs R2 of about 75% or more.
limits: Simulation, not real data. Authors and exact title were not recorded by this reader.
agent_relevance: A feature-only difficulty estimate is a prior, not a measurement. Update it with observed outcomes from the checks.

source: Peters et al. (2025) review, classification granularity
finding: Classification-style difficulty prediction is often off by one level rather than wildly wrong.
numbers: Exact accuracy 0.325-0.806 (mean 0.567, 3 studies). Adjacent accuracy 0.65 and 0.982 (2 studies). Yi et al. (2024) used three levels.
limits: Only two or three studies per number.
agent_relevance: A coarse easy/medium/hard split is a realistic target for S0.

source: Zotos et al. (2025) professor study, rater pooling
finding: Experts differ in how many items they refuse to rate, and averaging experts is no better than single raters.
numbers: Professor 3 gave no answer for 16 Neural Networks questions. Averaging the three professors (excluding the exam creator) gave no improvement.
limits: Four raters only.
agent_relevance: Votes from correlated raters add little, matching guardrail G4.

source: Acquaye et al. (2026) versus Li et al. (2026) on persona prompting
finding: Two papers disagree on persona prompting. Acquaye et al. get good results by pooling many persona runs. Li et al. find single personas unstable and only an average over personas helps.
numbers: Li et al.: the ensemble average over proficiencies improves alignment (their Table 2) while single-proficiency runs go up or down. Acquaye: classroom of 300 over 4 proficiency levels, r up to 0.82.
limits: Different datasets and labels (success rates on NAEP vs ranks on USMLE and SAT). The reconciliation is my reading, not a test.
agent_relevance: If a persona or probe is used, aggregate in code over many runs and never rely on one.
